title: Diagonalising: the same step, again and again

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is Dⁿ reading out as plain powers, with each tap only stretching the flag by 3 along (1, 0) and 2 along (−1, 1), when you step A again on the eigenvector grid.
interactive.title: Step it again
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in thirteen small screens. Most show the F-shaped flag you have seen before. A = [3 1; 0 2] moves it, the same matrix whose eigenvectors you found. A Step button applies A once more each tap. A counter n says how many steps have been taken. Back and Reset take it down again. A matrix card shows Aⁿ for the current n. The view zooms out by itself as the flag grows, so it stays in sight. A note gives the zoom. A grid switch swaps the square grid for the eigenvector grid. That grid's lines run along A's two eigenvectors, (1, 0) with eigenvalue 3 and (−1, 1) with eigenvalue 2. On it the flag is read as amounts of each. Each tap multiplies the first amount by 3 and the second by 2, because an eigenvector is only stretched. A second card then reads Dⁿ. It has the eigenvalues down its diagonal, with their powers worked out. Three presets load three matrices. They are the stretch [3 1; 0 2], the pumps [0.8 0.3; 0.2 0.7] and the shear [1 1; 0 1]. The pumps open a tanks view. Two tanks hold 1000 L between them, drawn as bars with their litres read out. Each tap is one hour of pumping. The shear draws only one eigenvector line. Its grid switch is greyed out, and the reason sits beside it. There is no second line to make a grid from. The screens. Screen 1 shows the stretch on the square grid. Three taps take the flag from n = 0 to n = 3. At n = 0 nothing has moved, so the card reads A⁰ = [1 0; 0 1]. Each time it leans further and grows. The card reads A = [3 1; 0 2], then A² = [9 5; 0 4], then A³ = [27 19; 0 8]. Each power is one more full multiplication. The finished picture shows the flag at n = 3. Screen 2 is a puzzle. (1, 0) is an eigenvector of A with eigenvalue 3. Where is it after four steps? It offers (81, 0), (12, 0) and (3, 0). (81, 0) is right, because each step multiplies by 3 again. Tapping four times checks it. Screen 3 turns the grid switch on. Three taps again. Each one stretches the flag 3 times along (1, 0) and 2 times along (−1, 1). A acts on each part separately, so A(a(1, 0) + b(−1, 1)) = 3a(1, 0) + 2b(−1, 1). The second card reads D⁰ = [1 0; 0 1], then D = [3 0; 0 2], then D² = [9 0; 0 4], then D³ = [27 0; 0 8]. After three steps the first amount has grown 27 times. The second has grown only 8 times. So the flag is drawn out more along (1, 0) than along (−1, 1). The finished picture shows the flag at n = 3 on the eigenvector grid. Screen 4 is a puzzle. The arrow (1, 1) is 2 lots of (1, 0) plus 1 lot of (−1, 1). So its amounts are (2, 1). What are they after three steps? It offers (54, 8), (6, 2) and (18, 6). (54, 8) is right, 2 × 27 and 1 × 8. Back on the square grid that is 54(1, 0) + 8(−1, 1) = (46, 8). Screen 5 shows P = [1 −1; 0 1], with the eigenvectors as its columns. P turns amounts on the eigenvector grid into your numbers. P⁻¹ = [1 1; 0 1] turns your numbers into amounts. Three panels follow (1, 1) through A = PDP⁻¹, right to left. P⁻¹ gives the amounts (2, 1). D stretches them to (6, 2). P turns that back into (4, 2), which is A(1, 1). The middle panel's axes are marked lots of (1, 0) and lots of (−1, 1). Unbalanced three-phase faults are worked out with the same move, called symmetrical components. The finished picture shows all three panels. Screen 6 is a puzzle. P's columns are taken the other way round, (−1, 1) first and (1, 0) second. What is D now? It offers [2 0; 0 3], [3 0; 0 2] and [3 1; 0 2]. [2 0; 0 3] is right, because each eigenvalue sits in the column of its own eigenvector. Screen 7 shows Aⁿ = PDⁿP⁻¹. A³ is PDP⁻¹ three times over. Each P⁻¹P in the middle is I, so it drops out. That leaves PD³P⁻¹. Worked out, [1 −1; 0 1][27 0; 0 8][1 1; 0 1] = [27 19; 0 8], the same as screen 1. In general PDⁿ = [3ⁿ −2ⁿ; 0 2ⁿ]. Multiplying by P⁻¹ = [1 1; 0 1] gives Aⁿ = [3ⁿ 3ⁿ − 2ⁿ; 0 2ⁿ]. The step counter runs on to n = 10. The card reads A¹⁰ = [59049 58025; 0 1024]. The finished picture shows n = 10. Screen 8 is a puzzle. Someone works out A³ as PDP⁻¹ and gets [3 1; 0 2]. What went wrong? The first choice says D was not cubed. The second says P and P⁻¹ should swap places. The third says nothing is wrong. The first is right. PDP⁻¹ is A itself, one step. With D cubed, PD³ = [27 −8; 0 8], and times P⁻¹ that is [27 19; 0 8]. Screen 9 shows the pumps in the tanks view. All 1000 L start in tank 1. Each hour the pump moves 20% of tank 1's water to tank 2. It also moves 30% of tank 2's water to tank 1. So A = [0.8 0.3; 0.2 0.7]. A(3, 2) = (3, 2) and A(1, −1) = (0.5, −0.5). So its eigenvalues are 1, with (3, 2), and 0.5, with (1, −1). The start, (1000, 0), is 200 lots of (3, 2) plus 400 lots of (1, −1). Each hour the first part stays as it is and the second halves. Four taps give tank 1 800, 700, 650 and 625 L. It heads for 200(3, 2) = (600, 400), a 60 : 40 split. A readout shows the part above 600 L. It reads 400, 200, 100, 50 and 25. The finished picture shows n = 4, with 625 L and 375 L. Screen 10 is a puzzle. How much is in tank 1 after five hours? It offers 612.5 L, 600 L and 625 L. 612.5 L is right, 600 + 400 × 0.5⁵ = 600 + 12.5. 600 L is where it heads, but it never quite gets there. 625 L is after four hours. Screen 11 shows the shear [1 1; 0 1]. det(A − λI) = (1 − λ)², so λ = 1 twice. But A − I = [0 1; 0 0] crushes only the line through (1, 0). One line cannot make a grid, so there is no P to invert. So λ = 1 has algebraic multiplicity 2 but geometric multiplicity 1. The grid switch is greyed out with that reason. Each tap pushes the flag further sideways. The card reads Aⁿ = [1 n; 0 1]. 2I also has its eigenvalue twice. Yet for 2I every line is an eigenvector line. The finished picture shows the shear at n = 3 with its one line. Screen 12 is a mixed puzzle. [2 1; 0 2] has the eigenvalue 2 twice. Can it be written as PDP⁻¹? The first choice says no, because it has only one eigenvector line. The second says yes, because it has two eigenvalues. The third says yes, because every 2 by 2 can. The first is right. A − 2I = [0 1; 0 0] crushes only the line through (1, 0). To be written as PDP⁻¹, a 2 by 2 needs two independent eigenvector lines. Screen 13 is a mixed puzzle. M = [0.7 0.2; 0.2 0.7] stretches (1, 1) by 0.9 and (1, −1) by 0.5. Start at (1, 0), which is half of each, and take 20 steps. Which line is the arrow nearly on? It offers the line through (1, 1), the line through (1, −1), and still the line through (1, 0). The first is right. After 20 steps the (1, 1) part is 0.5 × 0.9²⁰, about 0.06. The (1, −1) part is 0.5 × 0.5²⁰, less than a millionth. The picture shows the arrow shrinking onto the line through (1, 1). Some screens show an idea. The rest ask you to try it. Each puzzle offers three answers. On a narrow phone the answers and the readouts wrap onto more lines.
interactive.ignores: The view zooms out as the flag grows. So after many steps the flag is drawn far smaller than it really is. The tanks are pumped in whole-hour jumps to keep the sums plain. A real pump moves water all the time. After several hours the bars seem to settle at 600 L and 400 L. The readout still shows the small part left over. Each eigenvector line goes on for ever, past the panel's edge. The matrices and tank figures are example values.

explain.text:
Some changes repeat. Think of a pump that runs for an hour, every hour. Doing a matrix step n times means working out Aⁿ. Multiplying out powers is slow. It also hides where the steps are heading. The fix is to measure along the matrix's eigenvectors. On their grid each step only stretches each direction by its own eigenvalue. So n steps just raise each eigenvalue to the power n.[^1]

Take A = [3 1; 0 2] again. Its eigenvectors are (1, 0) with eigenvalue 3, and (−1, 1) with eigenvalue 2. Use those two arrows as your basis. A basis made of eigenvectors is an [[eigenbasis]]. The arrow (1, 1) is 2 lots of (1, 0) plus 1 lot of (−1, 1). So on this grid its amounts are (2, 1). A matrix acts on a mix part by part. So one step turns 2 lots of (1, 0) into 2 lots of A(1, 0). It turns 1 lot of (−1, 1) into 1 lot of A(−1, 1). Each eigenvector is only stretched. So the first amount is multiplied by 3, and the second by 2. So on this grid A acts as D = [3 0; 0 2]. D has the eigenvalues down its diagonal and zeros everywhere else. That makes it a [[diagonal matrix]]. Three steps give the amounts 2 × 27 and 1 × 8, which is (54, 8). Back on your grid that is 54(1, 0) + 8(−1, 1) = (46, 8).

Remember that one arrow can be read on two grids? Put the eigenvectors in as the columns of P = [1 −1; 0 1]. P turns amounts on the eigenvector grid into your numbers. P⁻¹ = [1 1; 0 1] turns your numbers into amounts. So A seen on the eigenvector grid is P⁻¹AP = D. Turned round, A = PDP⁻¹. Read it right to left. Go into the eigenvector grid, stretch, then come back out. To [[diagonalise]] A is to find this P and D. Each eigenvalue sits in the column of its own eigenvector. So swapping P's columns swaps D's entries.

Now repeat it. A³ is PDP⁻¹ PDP⁻¹ PDP⁻¹. Each P⁻¹P in the middle is I, which changes nothing. So A³ = PD³P⁻¹. In general Aⁿ = PDⁿP⁻¹. Dⁿ just raises each diagonal entry to the power n. Leave that power off and you get A itself, one step. Here Aⁿ = [3ⁿ 3ⁿ − 2ⁿ; 0 2ⁿ]. So A³ = [27 19; 0 8]. And A¹⁰ = [59049 58025; 0 1024], with no long multiplying.

The powers also show where the steps head. Each part is multiplied by its own eigenvalue every step. Say one eigenvalue is bigger in size than the rest. Then its part takes over, as long as the start has some of it. Take a pump that moves 20% of tank 1's water to tank 2 each hour. It also moves 30% of tank 2's water back. That is A = [0.8 0.3; 0.2 0.7]. Its eigenvalue is 1 along (3, 2) and 0.5 along (1, −1). Start with 1000 L, all in tank 1. That is 200 lots of (3, 2) plus 400 lots of (1, −1). Each hour the first part stays and the second halves. So tank 1 holds 800, 700, 650, then 625 L. It closes in on 600 L, a 60 : 40 split. It never quite gets there.

Not every matrix can be diagonalised. The grid needs as many independent eigenvectors as the matrix has columns. A shear such as [1 1; 0 1] has too few.[^2] Its eigenvalue 1 comes twice. But A − I = [0 1; 0 0] crushes only the line through (1, 0). One line makes no grid. So there is no P to invert. A repeated eigenvalue is not the trouble in itself. It is fine whenever you can still find enough independent eigenvectors.[^3] Take 2I. It has the eigenvalue 2 twice, and every nonzero arrow is one of its eigenvectors.

**Give a matrix enough independent eigenvectors and it is a plain stretch on their grid, P⁻¹AP = D. Then n steps are Aⁿ = PDⁿP⁻¹, with each eigenvalue raised to the power n.**[^1]

analogy.text: Picture two equal capacitors joined through a resistor. Look at them once a second. Charge only moves from one to the other. So the total never changes. That is the direction (1, 1), with eigenvalue 1. The difference between their charges shrinks by the same fraction every second. That is the direction (1, −1), with an eigenvalue below 1. Any start splits into a total part and a difference part. After n seconds the total is as it was. The difference has been multiplied by that fraction n times.
analogy.breaks: Real capacitors leak a little. So the total slowly falls too. And the rule only says where the charge is at each look. It says nothing about what happens between looks. Smooth change has its own form of this rule. There each eigenvalue is a rate, and e^(λt) takes the place of λⁿ.

practice.text:
- Find the eigenvalues from det(A − λI) = 0. Then find an eigenvector for each.
- Check you have as many independent eigenvectors as A has columns. If not, A cannot be diagonalised. Multiply out the powers instead.
- Put the eigenvectors in as the columns of P. Put each eigenvalue in D, in the same column as its eigenvector.
- Find P⁻¹. For a 2 by 2, swap the two diagonal entries, change the signs of the other two, and divide by the determinant.
- Check that AP = PD. Each column of AP should be its eigenvalue times that column of P.
- For n steps, raise each entry of D to the power n. Then work out PDⁿP⁻¹.

**Rules of thumb:** read PDP⁻¹ right to left. Go into the eigenvector grid, stretch, then come back out. When one eigenvalue is bigger in size than the rest, its part takes over in the end. That needs the start to have some of it. If every eigenvalue is smaller than 1 in size, every part dies away. Then Aⁿ heads for zero. An eigenvalue of exactly 1 gives a part that never changes, a steady state. A negative eigenvalue flips its part every step.

**Worked example:** the pumped tanks, A = [0.8 0.3; 0.2 0.7]. The eigenvectors are (3, 2) with eigenvalue 1, and (1, −1) with eigenvalue 0.5. So P = [3 1; 2 −1] and D = [1 0; 0 0.5]. det P = −3 − 2 = −5. So P⁻¹ = [0.2 0.2; 0.4 −0.6]. For three hours, D³ = [1 0; 0 0.125]. Then PD³ = [3 0.125; 2 −0.125]. And PD³P⁻¹ = [0.65 0.525; 0.35 0.475]. Start with 1000 L in tank 1. Three hours later tank 1 holds 650 L and tank 2 holds 350 L. Over many hours 0.5ⁿ heads for 0. So Aⁿ heads for [0.6 0.6; 0.4 0.4]. Whatever the start, the water heads for a 60 : 40 share.

**Where you meet it:** any rule of the form "next = A × now", stepped again and again. Symmetrical components rest on the same move. Engineers use them to work out unbalanced faults on three-phase systems. A change of basis turns a balanced system's matrix into a diagonal one.[^4] The new parts are called the positive, negative and zero sequences. Each part can then be worked on its own.

**Common mistakes**
- Leaving the power off D. PDP⁻¹ is A itself, one step.
- Getting the order wrong, as in PAP⁻¹ or P⁻¹DP. A = PDP⁻¹. P⁻¹ sits on the right, so it acts first.
- Putting D's eigenvalues in a different order from P's columns.
- Thinking a repeated eigenvalue always gives two eigenvectors. Count the independent lines, as with the shear.
- Thinking a repeated eigenvalue always rules it out. 2I has the eigenvalue 2 twice, and it is diagonal already.
- Expecting the tanks to reach 60 : 40 exactly. The part left over halves every hour. It never reaches zero.

sources.quote: Since all one of these matrices does is scale each basis vector by some eigenvalue, applying that matrix, say, 100 times will just correspond to scaling each basis vector by the 100th power of the corresponding eigenvalue

sources.quote: A shear, for example, doesn't have enough eigenvectors to span all of space
An n × n matrix with repeated eigenvalues can be diagonalized provided we can obtain n linearly independent eigenvectors
